issues.legal_issue: The enactment of a later succession law does not retrospectively enlarge an owner’s power to alienate ancestral property or nullify an earlier declaratory decree limiting the alienation.
material_facts: An owner had alienated ancestral property, and a declaratory decree obtained before the later succession law took effect provided that the alienation would not bind the estate beyond the owner’s lifetime.
The owner died after the succession law took effect.
The respondents argued that the succession law had made the owner a full owner and eliminated the basis for the earlier decree; they had not appealed the existing decree granting the sons a share.
issues.conclusion: The preliminary objection seeking dismissal of the suit in its entirety was rejected. The succession law did not retrospectively enlarge the owner’s power over the ancestral property or nullify the earlier decree, and the respondents could not challenge the unappealed award to the sons.
issues.legal_principle: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 does not retrospectively enlarge the power of a holder of ancestral land or nullify a decree passed before its enactment. The Court also relied on the fact that the respondents had not appealed the decree granting the sons a share. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.

rule.if: appeal_from_possession_decree and prior_declaratory_decree_limited_alienation_to_owner_lifetime and succession_law_took_effect_after_decree and respondents_did_not_appeal_existing_award

predicates.appeal_from_possession_decree: The case is an appeal concerning a decree for possession of property.
predicates.prior_declaratory_decree_limited_alienat: A court had declared that an alienation would not bind the owner’s estate beyond the owner’s lifetime.
predicates.succession_law_took_effect_after_decree: A succession law took effect after the declaratory decree was made.
predicates.respondents_did_not_appeal_existing_awar: The respondents did not appeal the existing award of a share to other claimants.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns possession, an earlier decree limited an alienation to the owner’s lifetime, a succession law took effect afterward, and the respondents did not appeal an existing award, the earlier decree remains effective.

issues.legal_issue: Heirs who could not challenge an ancestral-property alienation under the customary law may inherit property restored to the owner’s estate when succession opens under a later law.
material_facts: A son competent to challenge an alienation obtained a declaratory decree that the alienated property would not bind the estate beyond the owner’s lifetime.
The owner died after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 had taken effect, leaving sons, a widow, and daughters.
Under the prior customary law, the widow and daughters could not themselves challenge the alienation, but the succession law gave them equal inheritance rights.
issues.conclusion: The property reverted to the owner’s estate at death, and the sons, widow, and daughters were entitled to inherit it under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues.legal_principle: Under the customary law described by the Court, a declaratory decree obtained by a competent reversioner restored the alienated property to the alienor’s estate when the alienor died; it removed an obstacle to the rights of those entitled to succeed rather than making the alienation void from the outset. The restrictions in the Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1920, including sections 6 and 8, did not prevent women from inheriting when succession opened after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 took effect. Sections 2 and 4(1) of that Act governed the devolution of the estate. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.

predicates.possession_claim_based_on_prior_declarat: The claim for possession relies on a prior declaratory decree concerning the property.
predicates.competent_reversioner_obtained_decree_li: A person entitled under the then-applicable rules to challenge the alienation obtained a decree limiting its effect to the alienor’s lifetime.
predicates.alienor_died_after_equal_inheritance_law: The alienor died after a succession regime giving male and female heirs equal inheritance rights had taken effect.
predicates.women_heirs_were_barred_from_original_ch: Female heirs could not themselves bring the original challenge under the rules then governing the alienation.

issues.definition: When a possession claim rests on a qualifying declaratory decree, the alienor dies after equal inheritance rights take effect, and female heirs were barred from the original challenge, those female heirs inherit the property restored to the estate.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may grant relief to parties who did not appeal or file cross-objections when that relief is legally required to adjust rights among parties to the suit.
material_facts: The sons, daughters, and widow jointly sued for possession of the entire alienated property.
The trial court granted possession only of a share to the sons, and the district court granted the entire property to the sons alone.
The alienees appealed, while the widow and daughters did not appeal or file cross-objections.
The alienees failed to establish a subsisting interest in the property after the owner’s death, and the widow and daughters were legally entitled to shares.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court could adjust the rights of the sons, widow, and daughters and grant the widow and daughters their shares despite their failure to appeal or file cross-objections.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41, rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers an appellate court to pass a decree that ought in law to have been passed and to grant further or other relief required by the justice of the case, including in favour of parties who did not appeal or object. The Court explained that “which ought to have been passed” means what ought in law to have been passed. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.

predicates.appeal_from_decree_in_joint_possession_s: The case is an appeal from a decree in a suit brought jointly by multiple claimants for possession.
predicates.all_claimants_sought_entire_property: The claimants sought possession of the entire disputed property in the suit.
predicates.nonappealing_claimants_were_legally_enti: Claimants who did not appeal or object were legally entitled to shares in the property.
predicates.opposing_claimant_failed_to_establish_co: The opposing claimant failed to establish a continuing interest in the property.

issues.definition: When a joint possession suit sought the entire property, nonappealing claimants were legally entitled to shares, and the opposing claimant failed to establish a continuing interest, the appellate court may grant relief to those nonappealing claimants.
